questions.solution:
$C = \dfrac{Q}{V}$, in farads — the charge stored per volt.

It depends only on the geometry and the dielectric, not on how much charge happens to be on the plates.

questions.q: The energy stored in a capacitor is:
questions.solution:
$E = \tfrac12 QV = \tfrac12 CV^{2} = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C}$.

The $\tfrac12$ is there because the voltage rises from zero to $V$ as the capacitor charges, so the average voltage doing the work is $\dfrac{V}{2}$.

questions.q: For capacitors in series, the combined capacitance is found from:
questions.solution:
In **series** the reciprocals add — the opposite way round from resistors.

In **parallel** capacitances simply add, which is the resistor rule reversed as well.

questions.q: The force on a straight wire of length $L$ carrying current $I$ at angle $\theta$ to a field $B$ is:
questions.solution: $F = \mathbf{BIL\sin\theta}$ — greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field, and **zero** when it lies along it.

questions.q: A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences:
questions.solution:
$F = qvB\sin\theta$, and $\theta = 0$ gives **zero**.

A magnetic field acts only on motion that **cuts across** it — and even then the force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work.

questions.q: Find the charge (in $\mu$C) on a $10\,\mu$F capacitor charged to $12$ V.
Find the energy (in J) stored in a $200\,\mu$F capacitor at $100$ V.
Find the combined capacitance (in $\mu$F) of $4\,\mu$F and $6\,\mu$F in parallel.
Find the force (in N) on a $0.2$ m wire carrying $5$ A perpendicular to a $0.4$ T field.
Find the time constant (in s) of a circuit with $R = 2\,\text{M}\Omega$ and $C = 5\,\mu$F.
questions.solution:
$\tau = RC = 2 \times 10^{6} \times 5 \times 10^{-6} = \mathbf{10}$ s.

After one time constant the charge has fallen to $37\%$ of its initial value.

questions.q: Derive the exponential discharge equation for a capacitor, define the time constant, and explain how to find $RC$ from a graph.
questions.solution:
**Setting up.** A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor $R$. At any instant

$V = IR$ and $Q = CV$, and $I = -\dfrac{dQ}{dt}$ (negative because the charge is falling).

$-\dfrac{dQ}{dt}R = \dfrac{Q}{C}$

$\dfrac{dQ}{Q} = -\dfrac{dt}{RC}$

**Integrating:**

$\ln\dfrac{Q}{Q_{0}} = -\dfrac{t}{RC}$

$\mathbf{Q = Q_{0}e^{-t/RC}}$

The same form holds for $V$ and for $I$, since all three are proportional.

**The time constant** $\tau = RC$, in seconds, is the time for the charge to fall to $\dfrac{1}{e} = 37\%$ of its initial value.

After $2\tau$ about $14\%$ remains, after $5\tau$ less than $1\%$ — which is the usual working definition of 'fully discharged'.

**Finding $RC$ from a graph.** Take logarithms:

$\ln Q = \ln Q_{0} - \dfrac{t}{RC}$

Plot **$\ln Q$ against $t$**: a straight line of gradient $-\dfrac{1}{RC}$ and intercept $\ln Q_{0}$.

**Why the log plot is better** than reading the $37\%$ point off the curve: it uses **every** data point, averages out the random errors, and confirms that the decay really is exponential — a curve that fails to straighten was never exponential to begin with.

questions.q: Derive the radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a magnetic field, and explain why a magnetic field does no work.
questions.solution:
**Derivation.** For a charge moving perpendicular to the field, the magnetic force provides the centripetal force:

$qvB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$

$\mathbf{r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}} = \dfrac{p}{qB}$

**Reading the formula:** faster or heavier particles curve **less**; a stronger field or a larger charge curves them **more**.

**The period** is $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ — independent of speed and radius, which is the principle the cyclotron depends on.

**Why no work is done.** Work requires a force component **along** the displacement:

$W = Fs\cos\theta$

The magnetic force $q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ is always **perpendicular** to the velocity, so $\theta = 90°$ and $\cos\theta = 0$.

**Therefore the speed and kinetic energy never change** — only the direction does. A magnetic field is a perfect steering mechanism and a useless accelerator.

**A consequence worth stating:** this is why particle accelerators use **electric** fields to speed particles up and **magnetic** fields to bend them round the ring. Neither could do the other's job.

**And why the aurora exists:** charged particles from the Sun spiral along the Earth's field lines without gaining energy, and are funnelled towards the poles.

questions.q: Explain why capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel, and find the combined capacitance and energy stored when $6\,\mu$F and $3\,\mu$F in series are charged to $12$ V.
questions.solution:
**Why the rule is reversed.** In series, the same **charge** $Q$ sits on every capacitor — the inner plates are isolated, so whatever charge leaves one arrives on the next.

The **voltages add**:

$V = V_{1} + V_{2} = \dfrac{Q}{C_{1}} + \dfrac{Q}{C_{2}}$

$\dfrac{Q}{C} = Q\left(\dfrac{1}{C_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{C_{2}}\right)$

$\mathbf{\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{C_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{C_{2}}}$

The reciprocals add because $C$ sits in the **denominator** of $V = \dfrac{Q}{C}$, whereas $R$ sits in the numerator of $V = IR$. That single difference reverses both rules.

**The calculation.**

$\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac16 + \dfrac13 = \dfrac12$, so $C = \mathbf{2\,\mu}$F.

**Energy:**

$E = \tfrac12 CV^{2} = \tfrac12 \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 144 = \mathbf{1.44 \times 10^{-4}}$ J

**Checking by looking at each capacitor.** The charge on each is $Q = CV = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 12 = 24\,\mu$C.

$V_{1} = \dfrac{24}{6} = 4$ V and $V_{2} = \dfrac{24}{3} = 8$ V, which add to $12$ V ✓

**Note the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage** — the opposite of the resistor case, and worth remembering when choosing components by voltage rating.

questions.q: Explain the Hall effect, derive the Hall voltage, and give one application.
questions.solution:
**The effect.** A current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field perpendicular to the current. A potential difference appears **across** the conductor, perpendicular to **both** the current and the field.

**Why.** The moving charge carriers experience a magnetic force $qvB$ pushing them sideways. They accumulate on one face, leaving the opposite face with the opposite charge.

The separated charges set up a **transverse electric field**, which opposes further accumulation. Equilibrium is reached when the electric force balances the magnetic one:

$qE = qvB \Rightarrow E = vB$

Since $E = \dfrac{V_{H}}{d}$ across a slab of width $d$:

$V_{H} = vBd$

Substituting $I = nAvq$ with $A = dt$ (thickness $t$):

$\mathbf{V_{H} = \dfrac{BI}{ntq}}$

**Why the slab is thin.** $V_{H}$ is inversely proportional to $t$, so a thin specimen gives a bigger, more measurable voltage.

**Why a semiconductor rather than a metal.** $n$ is far smaller in a semiconductor, so the Hall voltage is thousands of times larger.

**Applications.**

1. **Hall probes** measure magnetic flux density directly, since $V_{H} \propto B$ with everything else fixed.

2. **Position and speed sensors** in cars and in brushless motors, detecting a passing magnet without contact.

3. **Determining the sign of the charge carriers** — the polarity of $V_{H}$ reveals whether they are negative (electrons) or positive (holes), which was historic evidence for hole conduction in semiconductors.

questions.q: Give three uses of capacitors, explaining the property of a capacitor that each depends on.
questions.solution:
**1. Smoothing a rectified supply.** After rectification the output is a series of humps rather than steady DC.

A capacitor across the output **charges at each peak and discharges slowly** through the load between peaks, filling in the dips. The ripple is reduced, and a larger $RC$ compared with the time between peaks means a smoother output.

**The property used:** a capacitor stores charge and releases it gradually.

**2. Timing circuits.** Charging or discharging through a resistor takes a predictable time $\tau = RC$.

Flashing indicators, delay circuits and the timing of a camera flash all use this. Changing $R$ or $C$ changes the interval, which is why such circuits are adjustable.

**The property used:** the exponential, calculable charging time.

**3. Delivering a large burst of energy.** A camera flash or a defibrillator charges a capacitor slowly from a small supply, then discharges it in **milliseconds**.

The energy is modest but the **power** is enormous, because $P = \dfrac{E}{t}$ and $t$ is tiny. A defibrillator delivers about $300$ J in $5$ ms — $60$ kW, which no battery could supply directly.

**The property used:** a capacitor can be discharged far faster than it is charged.

**4. Blocking DC while passing AC**, since a capacitor's reactance $\dfrac{1}{\omega C}$ is infinite at zero frequency — used to couple amplifier stages without passing their DC bias.

**A safety note:** a large capacitor in a television or a power supply holds a dangerous charge **long after the equipment is unplugged**, and must be deliberately discharged before anyone works on it.
